n: After Ahab’s treaty with Ben-hadad, three years of peace follow between Aram and Israel. Assyrian records suggest the two even fought side by side against Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC.
Jehoshaphat, the righteous king of Judah, visits Ahab. The two kingdoms are now allied, sealed by the marriage of Jehoshaphat’s son to Ahab’s daughter.

f.g: traveled north from Jerusalem’s heights; ‘down’ in elevation.

n: Ahab complains that Ramoth-gilead, an important fortress town east of the Jordan, is still held by Aram—apparently one of the cities Ben-hadad had promised to return.

f.g: a fortified city east of the Jordan and a city of refuge.

n: Ahab invites Jehoshaphat to join the campaign, and Jehoshaphat commits fully: “I am as you are.” Chronicles records that a prophet later rebuked him for this alliance.
Jehoshaphat wisely insists on seeking the Lord’s will first.

f.g: seek an answer from God through a prophet.

n: Ahab gathers about four hundred court prophets, who all say, “Go up.” They speak of “the Lord” (Adonai), not clearly naming Jehovah, and they tell the king what he wants to hear.

f.g: here Hebrew Adonai, a general title, rather than the covenant name Jehovah (LORD).

n: Jehoshaphat senses something is wrong and asks whether there is a true prophet of the LORD available.
Ahab admits there is one, Micaiah, but hates him because he never prophesies good for Ahab. Jehoshaphat gently objects.
Ahab sends an officer to bring Micaiah quickly.

f.g: a court official, perhaps a eunuch.

n: The two kings sit enthroned in royal robes at Samaria’s city gate, the public square of an ancient town, while the prophets perform.

f.g: an open area, a threshing floor.

n: Zedekiah, one of the court prophets, makes iron horns to act out the prophecy: Ahab will gore the Arameans like a bull.

f.g: gore, as an ox does with its horns.

n: All the prophets repeat the same encouraging message.
The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the others—pressure to conform.
Micaiah refuses: he will speak only what the Lord tells him. This is the mark of a true prophet.

f.w: what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak

n: At first Micaiah repeats the court prophets’ words—apparently with obvious sarcasm, since Ahab immediately sees through it.
Ahab demands the truth. Ironically, he insists on hearing what he has already decided to ignore.
Micaiah describes a vision: Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. In other words, the king will die, and his army will go home leaderless.

f.w: as sheep that have not a shepherd

n: Ahab turns to Jehoshaphat: “Didn’t I tell you?”
Micaiah reveals a heavenly council: the Lord enthroned and surrounded by the armies of heaven. Prophets often describe being shown God’s council.

f.w: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne

n: The Lord asks who will entice Ahab to go to his death at Ramoth-gilead. The council discusses ideas.
A spirit steps forward and volunteers.
The spirit will deceive Ahab through his prophets. Many readers understand this as God permitting the deception Ahab had already chosen to prefer, turning his love of flattery into his own judgment.
Micaiah declares plainly that the four hundred prophets are deceived, and disaster is decreed for Ahab.
Zedekiah slaps Micaiah and sneers, “Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go from me to you?”
Micaiah answers that Zedekiah will find out when he is hiding in an inner room in terror after the defeat.
Ahab orders Micaiah handed over to the city governor and a royal prince.
He is to be jailed on minimal rations until Ahab returns safely. It is a stubborn refusal to heed the warning.
Micaiah stakes his credibility on the outcome: if Ahab returns safely, the Lord has not spoken through him. He calls the people to witness. This is the biblical test of a prophet.

f.w: If thou return at all in peace

n: Both kings march on Ramoth-gilead anyway—even Jehoshaphat, who had heard the warning.
Ahab tries to cheat the prophecy by disguising himself as an ordinary soldier, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes—making Jehoshaphat the obvious target.
Ben-hadad orders his chariot commanders to target only the king of Israel. Ahab’s release of him three years earlier now comes back to haunt him.
Seeing Jehoshaphat’s royal robes, the chariots chase him. Jehoshaphat cries out—Chronicles adds that he cried to the Lord, who helped him.
Realizing he isn’t Ahab, they stop the pursuit.
An archer shoots at random, yet the arrow strikes Ahab precisely in the gap between his armor plates. No disguise can hide a man from God’s word.

f.g: at random, without aiming at anyone in particular.

f.w: between the joints of the harness
f.g: between the scales of his armor and the breastplate.

n: Ahab is propped up in his chariot all day to keep up morale, and dies at evening as his blood pools in the chariot.
At sunset the call goes out: “Every man to his home.” Israel is scattered, just as Micaiah saw.
Ahab is brought back to Samaria and buried.
When his chariot is washed at Samaria’s pool, dogs lick up his blood, fulfilling the prophecy. (The KJV’s “they washed his armour” is more likely “where the prostitutes bathed.”)

f.w: the dogs licked up his blood

f.g: the Hebrew likely means ‘and the harlots washed themselves there.’

n: Ahab’s building works included an “ivory house”—a palace decorated with ivory inlays. Archaeologists have found many carved ivories at Samaria.
Ahab dies; his son Ahaziah succeeds him.
The narrator now summarizes Jehoshaphat’s reign in Judah.
He was thirty-five at his accession and ruled twenty-five years (about 873–848 BC, including a co-regency with his father).
Jehoshaphat followed his father Asa’s good example, though local shrines remained in use.

f.w: the high places were not taken away

n: He ended the long hostility between Judah and Israel, partly through marriage alliance with Ahab’s family—a decision that would later bring Baal worship into Judah.

f.w: made peace with the king of Israel

n: Chronicles records much more of his reign, including his teaching program and judicial reforms.
He completed his father’s reform by removing the remaining shrine prostitutes.
Edom was then governed by a deputy under Judah’s control, which gave Judah access to the Red Sea port.

f.g: a governor appointed by Judah served as ruler.

n: Jehoshaphat tried to revive Solomon’s gold trade with Ophir, but his ships were wrecked in port at Ezion-geber. Chronicles says it was a judgment for allying with Ahab’s son.
Ahaziah of Israel offered to send his sailors too, but Jehoshaphat refused—perhaps having learned his lesson.
Jehoshaphat dies and his son Jehoram becomes king of Judah.
Ahab’s son Ahaziah begins a short two-year reign over Israel (about 853–852 BC).
He followed in the ways of his father Ahab, his mother Jezebel, and Jeroboam—three generations of false worship.
He served Baal as his father had. His story continues in 2 Kings 1, where he seeks a foreign god even on his sickbed.
